title: Automating report sending without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Client reports a person still checks
excerpt: Send the weekly number a client already expects, assembled on a schedule. A person writes the cause, and a failed fetch does not go out as a zero.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp. A weekly report is a number you already expect, checked under that lamp before it goes out.
caption: Two screens and a lamp. The number is checked before it leaves. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a weekly client report contain?
faqs.answer: One figure they already expect, a comparison with last week, and a link to the source. A sentence of cause only when a person has looked. If the source failed, send nothing or send a short note a person wrote, not a zero the template invented.

faqs.question: Can the report explain why a number dropped?
faqs.answer: Only after a person checks. The draft may state the figure and the delta, and it may not invent a cause such as a homepage change. "We do not know yet" is allowed, and a guessed cause is what you will have to retract.

faqs.question: Who should be on the recipient list?
faqs.answer: The people who are supposed to see that number, chosen by a person. Do not forward to everyone on the project by default. When the list changes, review it, because a new executive or a departed teammate is a disclosure decision.

sources.title: Influencing title links in Google Search

markdown:
Automated client reporting should deliver a number the client already expects, on the day you named, with a note only when a person has read the change. The report is a handoff, not a performance. If the figure is blank, late, or unexplained, do not send it and hope the prose will cover the gap.

Automate the assembly and the schedule. Keep a person on anything the client will see when the number moved in a way that needs a sentence, on anything that implies a decision about money, and on anything you would have to retract. A wrong explanation is harder to undo than a late report. Measure minutes of compiling against minutes of checking, and count explanations you had to take back.

## One number, one owner, one day

Pick the figure before you pick the tool. A weekly report that contains twelve charts is a magazine, and nobody asked for a magazine. Ask the client which number they already look for. Orders, uptime, open bugs, leads that a person has defined, a campaign total from a source you both trust. One primary figure. Two supporting figures at most. The rest can live in a link for the week someone wants to dig.

Name the source. "From the shop's order export, counted on Monday at 8" is a source. "From our analytics" is not, if three tools disagree. Agree what you will do when the source fails. The answer should be: send nothing, or send a note a person wrote that says the source failed. It should not be: send a zero.

Name the day. The value of a weekly number is that it arrives when they reach for it. A workflow that sends "when the data looks ready" will drift, and they will stop trusting the rhythm. If the day is wrong for a holiday, a person moves it and the note says why in one line.

Give the report an owner on your side who can answer a reply. A no-reply sender is appropriate only for a figure so stable that you truly do not expect questions. The first months are not that. Use a person.

## What the machine may assemble

The workflow may pull the agreed figures, place them in the template, and compare them to last week's figures so the reviewer can see the delta. It may draft a one-line description of the delta that quotes the numbers and does not give a cause. "Orders were 40, down from 52" is a description. "Orders fell because the new homepage confused people" is a cause, and the tool does not know the cause.

It may attach the export or the link to the dashboard view you trust. It may notify the owner that the draft is ready. It stops there.

It may not change the definition of the metric to make the week look smoother. It may not drop a bad day from the total. It may not combine two products so a decline disappears. Those are decisions about what the client is allowed to believe. A person makes them in the open, by changing the definition in writing, not by letting a draft quietly redefine the week.

If you include a sentence of context, a person writes it or approves a sentence that only restates the delta. Keep a library of allowed sentences if you want speed: "within the range of the last four weeks," "below last week, source attached," "source unavailable, no figure this week." A library is reviewable. Free prose is not.

## The subject line is the report

Most clients will read the subject and the first line, and only then decide to open the rest. Write the subject as a title that states the figure and the period. Google's documentation on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) makes the same demand of page titles: they should be clear and specific, and vague or repetitive titles do not help anyone choose. "Week of 4 May: 40 orders" is a title. "Your weekly insights are here" is a delay.

Put the number in the first line of the body as well, so a preview pane does not hide it. Then the comparison. Then the link. Then, only if a person added it, one sentence of context. A long narrative under a simple week teaches them that your reports are optional reading. You want the opposite. You want the number to be the habit, and the sentence to be rare enough that they notice when it appears.

Do not decorate the mail with a new banner, a quote, or a request for a referral. The report is the report. A second ask inside it makes the figure feel like bait, and they will trust the next one less.

## Causes, money, and other lines a person owns

When the number moves enough that a reasonable client will ask why, a person looks before the send. How much is "enough" is a threshold you set with them, or a threshold you are willing to defend. Inside that band, the template can go with the lighter check: right week, right client, source did not fail, no blank. Outside that band, the owner writes the sentence or explicitly decides there is nothing responsible to say yet. "We do not know why yet" is a permitted sentence. A guessed cause is not.

Do not let the report recommend a spend, a hire, or a redesign. Those are proposals. They belong in a conversation, priced and scoped, not in a Monday mail that looks like a measurement. If the figure suggests the work is off, the owner can offer to talk. The template does not prescribe the fix.

Do not send the same report to a list that has grown past the people who should see that number. Investors, new executives, and vendors get added by a person. A workflow that forwards "everyone on the project" will eventually include someone who left, or someone who should not see revenue. The recipient list is part of the review when it changes, and part of the setup when it does not.

If a figure is wrong and already sent, a person sends the correction, plainly, with the right number. Do not bury it in next week's mail and hope. Retracting a cause you stated is the same kind of note. The automation can draft the correction from the new export. The person who signed the original sends it.

An [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) is the right place to decide whether a weekly number is even the right promise. Bring the figure you think they need and the source it would come from. The studio can then say whether that handoff is a small automation or a distraction from the work.

## Minutes saved against minutes of checking

Time five reports built by hand, including the export, the argument about which dashboard is right, and the paragraph you rewrote. That argument about the source should happen once, in setup, not every week. If it still happens every week, you are not ready to automate the send. You are ready to pick a source.

Time the check on the automated draft. Right client, right week, source healthy, delta copied accurately, no cause you did not write. If the check takes longer than the old compile, the template is too ornate. Cut it back to the number, the comparison, and the link.

Count retractions. A month with a retraction means the lighter check was too light, or the source is unstable. Move back to a person writing the line, and keep the assembly. The assembly was the chore. The opinion was never the chore.

Also ask, once, whether the client uses it. A perfect report nobody opens is a candidate to shorten or to stop. Stopping is a successful measurement. You removed a ritual that had become a performance.

## When the week is bad, and when the feed is blank

A bad week still sends, if the number is true, unless a person is in the middle of a live incident and the mail would be noise or a leak. In an incident, a person decides what the client hears, and the weekly template waits. Do not let the schedule fire a cheerful frame around a figure that is bad because the site was down and you have not said so yet.

A blank week does not send the template with empty brackets or a zero you do not believe. The owner gets an internal alert. The client gets either nothing, if you have warned them that silence means a delayed source, or a short note a person sent. Agree which of those two you use, and write it down. Ambiguity here becomes a reputation for hiding.

Keep a short archive the client can open, so a lost email is not a fight about what the number was. The archive matches what you sent, including corrections. A dashboard that quietly changes last week's total without a note will break the habit you just built.

Review requests are a different send: you are asking for something, not delivering a number they expect. [Automating review requests without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-review-requests-without-losing-the-relationship) is the next piece, because the ask should wait until they have actually received the work, and it should stop if something is still wrong.
